evals.prompt: Our CI deploy role has this policy. Is it OK? {"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["iam:PassRole","ecs:RunTask","ecs:UpdateService","ecr:*"],"Resource":"*"}]} (Review the text only, do not run anything.)
expectations: Flags iam:PassRole on Resource * as a privilege-escalation risk
Explains the chain: PassRole plus ecs:RunTask lets it run a task as any role
Recommends restricting PassRole to specific role ARNs and iam:PassedToService
Recommends scoping ecr:* and the other resources instead of *

evals.prompt: Review this IAM role trust policy for GitHub Actions: {"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Federated":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity","Condition":{"StringLike":{"token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub":"repo:acme/*"}}}]} The role has AdministratorAccess because 'it is only for deploys'.
expectations: Flags that repo:acme/* lets any repository in the org assume the role
Recommends pinning sub to the specific repo and branch or environment
Notes the missing aud condition (sts.amazonaws.com)
Flags AdministratorAccess as too broad and recommends scoped permissions or separate plan/apply roles

evals.prompt: A vendor asked us to create a role they can assume. Their AWS account is 999988887777. We wrote Principal {"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::999988887777:root"} with sts:AssumeRole and attached ReadOnlyAccess. Anything missing?
expectations: Recommends an ExternalId condition to prevent the confused deputy problem
Notes that root principal trusts every principal in that account that is allowed to assume roles
Suggests limiting to specific vendor role or using least privilege instead of ReadOnlyAccess
Suggests session duration limits, logging or monitoring of AssumeRole

evals.prompt: A role in account A has s3:GetObject allowed on a bucket in account B, but gets AccessDenied. The bucket policy in B does not mention the role. Why?
expectations: Says cross-account access needs an Allow on both sides: identity policy in A and bucket policy in B
Says the bucket policy in B must allow the principal
Mentions other possible causes: explicit deny, SCP, permission boundary, KMS key policy or Block Public Access

evals.prompt: Reviewer said this statement is dangerous but it only has a Deny-ish feel: {"Effect":"Allow","NotAction":["iam:*","organizations:*"],"Resource":"*"}. Why is it dangerous?
expectations: Explains that Allow with NotAction allows everything except the listed actions
Notes it includes future AWS actions and nearly all services (effectively near-admin)
Recommends listing the allowed actions explicitly or using an SCP/Deny for guardrails

evals.prompt: Our developers use AdministratorAccess in the dev account 'to move fast'. How do we get to least privilege without breaking people?
expectations: Recommends measuring real usage with Access Analyzer or CloudTrail-generated policies or Access Advisor
Recommends iterating: start from observed use, test with simulation, monitor AccessDenied, keep rollback
Suggests guardrails like permission boundaries or SCPs, and separate break-glass or time-bound elevation
Does not recommend removing admin immediately in one step

evals.prompt: We run workloads on GCP and CI deploys using a downloaded service account JSON key stored in GitHub secrets, with roles/editor on the project. What would you change?
expectations: Recommends Workload Identity Federation instead of a downloaded key
Recommends replacing roles/editor with predefined or custom least-privilege roles
Mentions iam.serviceAccounts.actAs or token creator as escalation to watch
Recommends disabling or auditing user-managed service account keys (org policy)

evals.prompt: Our Azure pipeline service principal has Owner at the subscription scope and a client secret that never expires. Risks and fix?
expectations: Flags Owner at subscription as able to grant any access (role assignment) and too broad
Recommends least-privilege role at a narrower scope, such as Contributor on a resource group
Recommends managed identity or workload identity federation instead of a long-lived client secret
Mentions secret expiry/rotation or credential inventory

evals.prompt: Review these policies before we use them in production: statement 1 allows Action * on Resource *; statement 2 allows iam:CreatePolicyVersion and iam:AttachRolePolicy on *; statement 3 is a bucket policy with Principal * and s3:GetObject without conditions; statement 4 is an SNS service-principal resource policy without aws:SourceArn. (Text only.)
expectations: Flags Action * on Resource * as full admin
Flags CreatePolicyVersion and AttachRolePolicy on * as privilege escalation
Flags Principal * without conditions as public access needing justification
Flags missing aws:SourceArn/SourceAccount as confused deputy risk
